query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Cr content (or adding other oxidation‐resistant elements such as Ti, Al, and Si) in high-entropy alloys will improve oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous protective oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy or refractory alloy with a baseline composition containing moderate levels of oxidation‐sensitive elements.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by increasing the concentration of Cr (and possibly Ti, Al, and Si) during synthesis.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure in an oxidizing environment (e.g., air at temperatures around 800°C or higher).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, continuous Cr-based oxide (such as Cr2O3) film on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The added Cr preferentially oxidizes to form a stable, adherent oxide scale that serves as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, thereby slowing down further oxidation of the underlying material.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will show a reduced oxidation rate (lower oxide scale thickness and weight gain during oxidation tests) compared to the baseline alloy with lower Cr content.
generation.baseline: The oxidation behavior of the original high-entropy alloy with standard Cr and related element levels.
generation.boundary: This method is expected to be effective under high-temperature oxidizing conditions where a protective oxide scale can be maintained; however, benefits may be limited if competing phase formations or scale spallation occur at excessively high temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal concentration of Cr and the potential trade-offs with other mechanical properties remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of sample alloys: one with the baseline composition and one with an increased Cr (and/or Ti, Al, Si) content. Subject both sets to an isothermal oxidation test in air at a high temperature (e.g., 800°C) for an extended period (e.g., 100 hours). Post-test, perform detailed microstructural and compositional analyses (SEM/EDS and XRD) to assess oxide scale formation and measure weight gains.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness (via cross-sectional SEM imaging)
Weight gain during oxidation (using thermogravimetric analysis)
Phase identification in the scale (using XRD)
Elemental composition of the oxide layer (using EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with increased Cr (and/or Ti, Al, Si) exhibits no statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., similar or higher oxide scale thickness and weight gain) compared to the baseline sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
